items.stem: An architect must let a partner organization's staff sign in with their own corporate identities, without creating local accounts. Which design best fits?

options.text: Identity federation with a trusted external identity provider
options.rationale: Correct: federation lets the partner authenticate users at their own IdP and assert identity to your systems.

options.text: Creating shared local accounts for the partner team
options.rationale: Shared accounts break accountability and are explicitly discouraged.
Removing authentication eliminates the control entirely.

options.text: Emailing a single password to all partner staff
options.rationale: A shared emailed password is neither auditable nor revocable per user.

items.explanation: Correct: federation lets the partner authenticate users at their own IdP and assert identity to your systems.

items.stem: Which control model grants access based on evaluated attributes such as department, location and time rather than fixed role names?

options.rationale: Correct: ABAC evaluates attributes/policies at access time.
RBAC assigns permissions to named roles, not evaluated attributes.

options.text: MAC enforced solely by file owners
options.rationale: Owner-set permissions describe discretionary control, not attribute policy.
This describes an absence of control, not a model.

items.explanation: Correct: ABAC evaluates attributes/policies at access time.

items.stem: Select TWO responsibilities that belong to a sound cryptographic key-management architecture.

options.text: Defining key rotation and expiry schedules
options.rationale: Correct: rotation limits exposure if a key is compromised.

options.text: Restricting and auditing access to key material
options.rationale: Correct: controlling who can use keys is central to key management.

options.text: Hard-coding keys into application source code
options.rationale: Embedding keys in source exposes them in repositories and builds.

options.text: Reusing one key for every system indefinitely
options.rationale: A single never-rotated key maximizes blast radius on compromise.

options.text: Publishing private keys to simplify integration
options.rationale: Private keys must never be published; doing so defeats the control.

items.explanation: Correct: rotation limits exposure if a key is compromised. Correct: controlling who can use keys is central to key management.
